'''Riffle''' is an [[anonymity network]] developed by researchers at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] and [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]] as a response to the problems of the [[Tor (anonymity network)|Tor network]].

== Overview ==
Riffle employs a [[privacy]]-enhancing [[Communication protocol|protocol]] that provides strong [[anonymity]] for secure and anonymous communication within groups. The protocol is designed using the anytrust model, which ensures that even if colluding [[Server (computing)|servers]] attempt to compromise the privacy of the group, they cannot do so if at least one server in the group is honest.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Uchill |first=Joe |date=2016-07-11 |title=Researchers tout new anonymity network |url=https://thehill.com/policy/cybersecurity/287255-researchers-tout-new-anonymity-network |access-date=2021-02-12 |website=TheHill |language=en}}</ref>

Like Tor, it utilizes [[onion routing]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Francisco |first=Iain Thomson in San |title=Meet Riffle, the next-gen anonymity network that hopes to trounce Tor |url=https://www.theregister.com/2016/07/13/riffle_next_gen_anonymity/ |access-date=2021-02-12 |website=www.theregister.com |language=en}}</ref> According to MIT's Larry Hardesty, researchers at MIT and the [[Qatar Computing Research Institute]] demonstrated a vulnerability in Tor's design.<ref>{{cite web |author=Larry Hardesty |date=11 July 2016 |title=How to stay anonymous online |url=https://news.mit.edu/2016/stay-anonymous-online-0711 |publisher=MIT News}}</ref>

== Technical design ==
To achieve its goals, Riffle implements two distinct protocols: the Hybrid Shuffle protocol for sending and [[Private Information Retrieval]] (PIR) for receiving.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Kwon |first1=Albert |last2=Lazar |first2=David |last3=Devadas |first3=Srinivas |last4=Ford |first4=Bryan |date=1 April 2016 |title=Riffle: An Efficient Communication System With Strong Anonymity |url=http://people.csail.mit.edu/devadas/pubs/riffle.pdf |journal=Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies |volume=2 |pages=115–134 |doi=10.1515/popets-2016-0008 |hdl=1721.1/128773 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

For sending information, Riffle uses a hybrid shuffle, consisted of a verifiable shuffle and a [[symmetric-key algorithm]]. The Hybrid Shuffle protocol consists of a setup phase and a transmission phase. During the setup phase, a slow verifiable shuffle based on [[Public-key cryptography|public key cryptography]] is used, while an efficient shuffle based on [[Symmetric-key cryptography|symmetric key cryptography]] is used during the transmission phase.<ref name=":0" /> Messages sent over Riffle are not forwarded if they have been altered by a compromised server. The server has to attach [[Zero-knowledge proof|proof]] in order to forward the message. If a server encounters [[Authentication protocol|unauthenticated]] messages or different permutations, it exposes the [[Digital signature|signed]] message of the previous server and runs the accusation protocol to ensure [[Authentication|verifiability]] without requiring computationally intensive protocols during transmission phases.<ref name=":0" />

For receiving information it utilizes multi-server [[Private information retrieval|Private Information Retrieval]]. All servers in the system share a [[replicated database]], and when a [[Client–server model|client]] requests an entry from the [[database]], they can cooperatively access it without knowing which entry they are accessing.<ref name=":0" />

== Use cases ==

<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Riffle-anonymous-file-sharing.jpg]] -->

The main intended [[Use case|use-case]] is anonymous [[file sharing]]. According to the lead project researcher, Riffle is intended to be complementary to Tor, not a replacement.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2016-08-31|title=Building a new Tor that can resist next-generation state surveillance|url=https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2016/08/building-a-new-tor-that-withstands-next-generation-state-surveillance/|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2021-02-12|website=Ars Technica|language=en-us}}</ref>
